findings.description: The RDS instance sets publicly_accessible = true, giving it a public IP and exposing the MySQL endpoint to the internet rather than keeping it private to the VPC.
storage_encrypted = false means the database volumes and snapshots store data unencrypted, exposing sensitive data if the underlying storage or a snapshot is accessed.

The master password is supplied via var.password and the username is hardcoded to the well-known 'admin'; the password is written to Terraform state in plaintext and reused in EC2 user_data, and no IAM database authentication is enabled.

The parameter group attached does not set require_secure_transport, and no TLS enforcement is configured, so client connections (the PHP app uses plain mysqli_connect) may traverse the network unencrypted.

The database master password is interpolated into the instance user_data script, which is stored unencrypted in the Terraform state and retrievable by anyone with access to the instance metadata service (169.254.169.254/latest/user-data) or ec2:DescribeInstanceAttribute.

No metadata_options block requiring http_tokens = "required" is set, so IMDSv1 remains usable; combined with the credentials in user_data and the overly permissive instance profile, an SSRF in the PHP app could yield role credentials and the DB password.
No root_block_device/ebs encryption is configured, so the instance volume holding the credentials file /var/www/inc/dbinfo.inc is stored unencrypted.
The inline policy grants s3:*, ec2:*, and rds:* on Resource "*", allowing the EC2 instance (and anyone compromising the web app) full control of all S3 buckets, EC2, and RDS resources in the account.
The database security group allows all outbound traffic to 0.0.0.0/0 on every protocol and port, facilitating data exfiltration from a compromised database host.

The attached ingress rule opens port 3306 to the entire VPC CIDR rather than just the application security group, letting any instance in the VPC reach the database; combined with publicly_accessible = true this widens exposure further.
The database endpoint of a publicly accessible, unencrypted RDS instance is exported as a plain (non-sensitive) output, aiding discovery by anyone with state or CI log access.
